log.why: Knocking out lacZ and katG splits the prior probability mass almost evenly (0.460 vs 0.540), maximizing information gain.
Treating at 3 uM roughly bisects the prior probability distribution (0.593 vs 0.407) to maximize information gain.
E5 narrowed the culprit to lacZ or katG; testing katG directly will resolve the top two candidates.
Testing at 10 uM splits the remaining posterior mass nearly in half (0.51 vs 0.49) and directly tests the leading hypothesis.
Test lacZ directly on Ticket 1 to confirm the 0.751 posterior and avoid a costly retraction before publishing.
Test the two highest-probability genes (fliC and gyrA, combined 0.544 posterior) on Ticket 3 while Ticket 1 incubates.
Ticket 1 has a 97.1% posterior for lacZ and is running low on time.
Test gyrA directly to distinguish between the two remaining likely candidates, gyrA and fliC.
Both E3 (no response at 3 µM) and E4 (response at 10 µM) bracket the threshold at 10 µM with sufficient confidence before time runs low.
Test {recA, dnaK} on Ticket 4 (combined prior 0.502) so it can incubate while we publish Ticket 3.
gyrA has a 0.937 posterior after two positive knockout results and time is running low.
Ticket 4 has only 30s left and metJ is at 0.523; testing E5 directly confirms or refutes metJ before publishing.
E4 splits Ticket 5's prior nearly in half while we wait for Ticket 4's E5 result.
E5 tests whether the dose threshold is at or below 30 µM, splitting the remaining high-probability hypotheses.
With 21s left, running E5 on Ticket 6 tests the 30 µM threshold while E5 finishes on Ticket 5, leaving time to publish both.
With only 3 seconds left in the round, we attempt to publish Ticket 5 as it has a strong 0.726 posterior for 30 µM.
